chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows one school day. Clocks on the wall, a race on the track and a notice board are the places where time is read, measured and changed from one unit to another. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.title: Videos teach, tools explore
points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student explores, builds and checks the idea alone, with hints, retry and reset. Five tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own plan.

points.title: A tool in three steps
points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own question, used exactly as the book gives it.

points.title: Every book question has its own video
points.text: Every solved example, Let Us Do question and every answerable prompt of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.

points.title: The picture is the mathematics
points.text: Clock faces, a strip for the whole day, time lines and double number lines carry each idea: every clock has the same three hands in the same three colours, and the time being asked about is the largest thing on screen.

points.title: Only the book's numbers
points.text: Every time, every clock and every question is the book's own. Any number the plan adds is a practice value and is said to be one.

design_references.text: priority_doc.md (the plan written to the 'Class 5 Mathematics Learning Experience Designer' brief, 2026-11-06): topic flow, video types, the 5 tools, the shared visual language and the learning rules decide this chapter's design.

docs/01_runbook.md and .claude/skills/lp/SKILL.md: framing intro with a free-try tool, idea topics each ending in a Practice concept, a Questions topic after every idea topic with a question concept and an answer concept per book question, and one summary topic.

modules.module_name: Clock Time, Time Elapsed and Two Ways to Write the Time
modules.module_summary: Reading a clock, finding how much time has passed between two times, comparing times taken, and writing a time in the 12-hour and the 24-hour format.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Raghav looks at the wall clock when he starts his yoga and again when he finishes. Will the hands of the clock be in the same places both times?
2. Raghav practices yoga in the morning.
3. Before he begins, he stands on his mat and looks at the wall clock. When he finishes, he sits on the mat and looks at the clock again.
4. The hands are in different places on the two clocks. How much time went by? Think about it, then try it with two clocks on the next screen.

tool_config.title: Yoga Clock
tool_config.idea: Set a Start clock and a Finish clock, read the time on each, and read how much time lies between them from the shaded stretch that grows when the Finish minute hand moves forward.
tool_config.screen: Raghav's yoga room, drawn as a warm, polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation: a wooden floor, a yoga mat and, on the wall above it, two large analogue wall clocks side by side, named Start and Finish. The two clocks are the largest things on screen. Each clock has a dark teal rim, a pale face, every number from 1 to 12, 60 small marks, a blue hour hand and an orange minute hand, and the hour hand moves a little as the minute hand moves, like a real clock. Under each clock sits a digital read-out, hh:mm, with a switch beside it that shows a sun for a.m. and a moon for p.m. A pale orange shaded stretch grows on the Finish clock from the Start position to the Finish position as the student moves the Finish minute hand forward, and a stretch longer than 1 hour goes round again in a thin outer ring. Below the clocks a time spent box has two small number boxes, hours and minutes (the hours box can stay empty), with a large number pad and a Check button. Controls: drag the minute hand of either clock (the hour hand follows), tap the sun and moon switch of a clock, and type in the time spent box. On the cards where the tool sets the clocks, the digital read-outs are hidden and the student types the start time, the finish time and the time spent instead. Fixed controls: Hint, Retry (resets the clocks of this card), Reset (returns both clocks to the start of the tool), Back and Next in the same places on every card, and 6 progress dots, with a one-sentence instruction strip at the top and a counter showing the card number out of 6.
student_does: Look at Raghav on his mat with the two wall clocks from the story. Set the Start clock to where it was when Raghav began and the Finish clock to where it was when he stopped, and say what you notice.

Set the Start clock and the Finish clock to the times on each card, read the shaded stretch and the time spent, then read two clocks that the tool sets and type the start time, the finish time and the time spent (practice values).
Read the two wall clocks of Raghav's yoga from the story, shown with hands only, and type the start time, the finish time and the time spent.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): set the Start clock to 07:10 a.m. and the Finish clock to 07:40 a.m., then read the shaded stretch. How much time is between them? Answer: 30 minutes, because the minute hand moves from 2 to 8, that is 6 numbers, and 6 × 5 = 30 minutes.

Card 2 (practice values): set the Start clock to 09:35 a.m. and the Finish clock to 10:10 a.m. The shaded stretch passes the number 12. How much time is between them? Answer: 35 minutes, because 09:35 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. is 60 − 35 = 25 minutes, 10:00 a.m. to 10:10 a.m. is 10 minutes, and 25 + 10 = 35 minutes.

Card 3 (practice values): set the Start clock to 08:00 a.m. and the Finish clock to 09:15 a.m. The shaded stretch goes once round and a little more. How much time is between them? Answer: 1 hour 15 minutes, because 08:00 a.m. to 09:00 a.m. is 1 hour and 09:00 a.m. to 09:15 a.m. is 15 minutes.

Card 4 (practice values): set the Start clock to 06:20 a.m. and the Finish clock to 07:05 a.m. How much time is between them? Answer: 45 minutes, because 06:20 a.m. to 07:00 a.m. is 60 − 20 = 40 minutes, 07:00 a.m. to 07:05 a.m. is 5 minutes, and 40 + 5 = 45 minutes.

Card 5 (practice values): the tool sets the clocks for an evening. The Start clock has the hour hand between 7 and 8 and the minute hand on 3. The Finish clock has the hour hand between 7 and 8 and the minute hand on 11. Switch both to the moon, then type the start time, the finish time and the time spent. Answer: 07:15 p.m., 07:55 p.m. and 40 minutes, because 3 × 5 = 15, 11 × 5 = 55 and 55 − 15 = 40 minutes.

Challenge: 'Raghav practices yoga in the morning.' The two wall clocks of the story are shown with hands only: the first has the hour hand between 5 and 6 and the minute hand on 7, and the second has the hour hand just before 6 and the minute hand on 11. 'At what time did Raghav start practising Yoga? At what time did he finish? How much time did he spend practising Yoga?' The student reads both clocks and types the three answers. Answers: 05:35 a.m., 05:55 a.m. and 20 minutes, because 7 × 5 = 35, 11 × 5 = 55 and 55 − 35 = 20 minutes.
feedback: A wrong minute reading gets a soft amber note with the reason, never red. For the story's Start clock: the minute hand points at 7, so that is 7 × 5 = 35 minutes past.
A wrong hour reading says which hand to look at: the short blue hand shows the hour, and the hour is the number it has just passed, so between 5 and 6 the hour is 5.
A morning time typed with p.m. gets a note about the switch: the sun means a.m., the morning, and the moon means p.m., the afternoon or evening.
A solved card shows how the stretch was counted, for example: 09:35 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. is 25 minutes and 10:00 a.m. to 10:10 a.m. is 10 minutes, so 25 + 10 = 35 minutes.
A time spent that mixes up minutes and hours, such as 15 hours for 15 minutes, gets a note to look at the shaded stretch: if the minute hand has not gone round, the time is less than 1 hour.
tool_config.done_when: All 6 cards are done, the three answers about Raghav's yoga are read correctly from the clocks, and the last card is finished without a bottom-out hint.

hint_ladder.text: Which hand tells the hour and which hand tells the minutes? Look at the short blue hand and the long orange hand.
Each number on the dial is 5 minutes. Count the minutes in fives from 12 to where the long hand points.
Look at the long orange hand on your clock: how many numbers past 12 is it? Multiply that number by 5 to get the minutes.
Worked step on a practice clock: the short hand is between 8 and 9, so the hour is 8. The long hand is on 4, and 4 × 5 = 20 minutes, so the time is 08:20. Do the same with your clock.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Remo began reading at 03:10 p.m. and stopped at 03:50 p.m. Did he read for more than 1 hour or for less than 1 hour?
2. Less than 1 hour. Both times are in the same hour, 3, so take the smaller minutes from the bigger minutes: 50 − 10 = 40 minutes.
3. To read a clock: the short blue hand shows the hour and the long orange hand shows the minutes. Each number on the dial is 5 minutes, so the minute hand on 4 means 4 × 5 = 20 minutes, not 4 minutes.
4. Same minutes: count the hours. 02:20 p.m. to 06:20 p.m. is 6 − 2 = 4 hours.
5. Different hours and minutes: hop to the next whole hour, then hop whole hours, then add the rest. 1 hour is 60 minutes, so 10:35 a.m. to 11:00 a.m. is 60 − 35 = 25 minutes. You can also hop whole hours first and then the rest.
6. Rule: start at the earlier time and count up to the later time in easy hops.

content.text:
Worked example: Zainab started colouring at 04:25 p.m. and stopped at 05:10 p.m. (a) How long did she colour? Then: (b) How long is it from 07:20 a.m. to 10:50 a.m.?
1. (a) Hop to the next whole hour. 04:25 p.m. to 05:00 p.m. is 60 − 25 = 35 minutes.
2. 05:00 p.m. to 05:10 p.m. is 10 minutes.
3. 35 + 10 = 45 minutes, so Zainab coloured for 45 minutes.
4. (b) Hop whole hours first. 07:20 a.m. to 10:20 a.m. is 10 − 7 = 3 hours.
5. 10:20 a.m. to 10:50 a.m. is 50 − 20 = 30 minutes.
6. So the time from 07:20 a.m. to 10:50 a.m. is 3 hours 30 minutes.
7. Check: 07:20 a.m. plus 3 hours is 10:20 a.m., and 10:20 a.m. plus 30 minutes is 10:50 a.m.
Answer: (a) 45 minutes (b) 3 hours 30 minutes

content.text:
1. Predict first: Akira took 1 hour 55 minutes and Sunita took 2 hours 5 minutes to paint a picture. Who took longer?
2. Sunita took longer. Look at the hours first: Sunita has 2 hours and Akira has only 1 hour. The minutes only matter when the hours are the same.
3. Check in minutes: 1 hour 55 minutes is 60 + 55 = 115 minutes and 2 hours 5 minutes is 120 + 5 = 125 minutes. 125 is more than 115.
4. When the hours are the same, compare the minutes: 2 hours 10 minutes is less than 2 hours 40 minutes, because 10 is less than 40.
5. Rule: compare the hours first. If the hours are the same, compare the minutes. The longest time is the biggest and the least time is the smallest.

Worked example: Zainab took 1 hour 50 minutes, Remo took 1 hour 25 minutes and Mary took 2 hours 5 minutes to finish a puzzle. Who took the longest time and who took the least?
1. Compare the hours first. Zainab has 1 hour, Remo has 1 hour and Mary has 2 hours.
2. Mary has the most hours, so Mary took the longest time.
3. Zainab and Remo have the same hours, so compare their minutes.
4. 25 minutes is less than 50 minutes, so Remo took less time than Zainab. Remo took the least time.
5. Check in minutes: Zainab 60 + 50 = 110, Remo 60 + 25 = 85 and Mary 120 + 5 = 125.
6. 125 is the most and 85 is the least, so Mary is the longest and Remo is the least.
Answer: Mary took the longest time and Remo took the least time

concepts.concept_name: Two Ways to Write the Time

content.text:
1. Predict first: a day has 24 hours, but a 12-hour clock only counts up to 12. How does it tell 05:30 in the morning from 05:30 in the evening?
2. It adds a.m. or p.m. A day has 24 hours, so the 12-hour clock goes round twice. The first round is the morning (a.m.). The second round is the afternoon and evening (p.m.).
3. The 24-hour format counts once, from 00:00 to 24:00. It does not use a.m. or p.m. It writes the word hours after the time.
4. A morning time keeps its digits: 05:30 a.m. is 05:30 hours.
5. For a p.m. time, add 12 to the hour: 02:30 p.m. is 2 + 12 = 14, so it is 14:30 hours.
6. The minutes never change. To go back from a 24-hour time above 12, take 12 away from the hour.
7. Rule: a morning time keeps its digits. For a p.m. time, add 12 to the hour. The minutes stay the same.

content.text:
Worked example: (a) Write 07:45 p.m. in the 24-hour format. (b) Write 16:20 hours in the 12-hour format.
1. (a) 07:45 p.m. is a p.m. time, so add 12 to the hour.
2. 7 + 12 = 19.
3. The minutes stay 45, so 07:45 p.m. is 19:45 hours.
4. (b) 16 is more than 12, so it is a p.m. time. Take 12 away from the hour.
5. 16 − 12 = 4.
6. The minutes stay 20, so 16:20 hours is 04:20 p.m.
7. Check: going back, 4 + 12 = 16 and 19 − 12 = 7, so both answers match.
Answer: (a) 19:45 hours (b) 04:20 p.m.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Raghu's art class starts at 15:20 hours and ends at 17:05 hours. Is it longer than 2 hours or shorter than 2 hours?
2. Shorter. With 24-hour times there is no a.m. or p.m. to keep track of, so just count up from the earlier time to the later time.
3. Hop to the next whole hour: 15:20 hours to 16:00 hours is 60 − 20 = 40 minutes.
4. Hop whole hours: 16:00 hours to 17:00 hours is 17 − 16 = 1 hour.
5. Add the rest: 17:00 hours to 17:05 hours is 5 minutes. 40 + 5 = 45 minutes, so the class lasts 1 hour 45 minutes. That is shorter than 2 hours.
6. Hop in your head instead of subtracting in columns, because an hour has 60 minutes and not 100.
7. Rule: go to the next whole hour, add the whole hours, then add the rest of the minutes.

content.text:
Worked example: A drawing class starts at 13:40 hours and ends at 16:15 hours. How long does it last?
1. 13:40 hours to 14:00 hours is 60 − 40 = 20 minutes.
2. 14:00 hours to 16:00 hours is 16 − 14 = 2 hours.
3. 16:00 hours to 16:15 hours is 15 minutes.
4. 20 + 15 = 35 minutes.
5. So the drawing class lasts 2 hours 35 minutes.
6. Check: 13:40 hours plus 2 hours is 15:40 hours, and 15:40 hours plus 35 minutes is 16:15 hours.
Answer: 2 hours 35 minutes

content.text:
A morning time keeps its digits in the 24-hour format. A p.m. time adds 12 to the hour. The minutes never change.
To go back from a 24-hour time above 12 to a p.m. time, take 12 away from the hour.
To find the time between two 24-hour times, hop to the next whole hour, then whole hours, then the rest.

tool_config.title: Day Strip
tool_config.idea: Place a time on a strip of the whole day, read it in the 12-hour and in the 24-hour format, and see that a p.m. time sits 12 hours further along the strip than its morning twin; two markers show the time between two 24-hour times.
tool_config.screen: The school notice board, drawn as a warm, polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A long timetable strip for one whole day is pinned across the board and is the largest thing on screen. The strip has 24 hour boxes numbered 00 to 23 from left to right, the a.m. side (00 to 11) under a sun and the p.m. side (12 to 23) under a moon, with the two ends labelled 00:00 and 24:00. Two draggable markers sit on the strip, named First time and Second time, and each marker has a small analogue clock above it (blue hour hand, orange minute hand, 60 small marks) that follows the marker. Two read-outs sit under the strip for the selected marker: the 12-hour read-out, hh:mm a.m. or p.m., and the 24-hour read-out, hh:mm hours. A gap bar between the two markers shows the time between them in hours and minutes. Controls: drag a marker along the strip (it snaps to 5 minutes and stays between 01:00 hours and 23:55 hours), tap a read-out to type a time with a large number pad, a switch named Show the 12 added that draws a +12 bracket over the p.m. side, and a Check button. On a gap card the 12-hour read-out is hidden, because the gap is read in 24-hour time. For the book's match question the strip is replaced by two columns of boxes and the student taps a 12-hour time and then its 24-hour time to draw a line between them. Fixed controls: Hint, Retry (returns the markers of this card), Reset (clears both markers), Back and Next in the same places on every card, and 7 progress dots, with a one-sentence instruction strip at the top and a counter showing the card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at the strip with one morning time and one afternoon time marked, each with its 24-hour name. Drag the marker to each time and read both boxes before you press Check.

Drag the marker to a time and read both boxes, turn on the +12 bracket for a p.m. time, type the 12-hour time for a given 24-hour time, and put two markers on the strip to read the gap between them (practice values).
Fill the book's table of the 12-hour and 24-hour formats, match its six pairs, and find how long Raghu took to reach his Nana ji's house.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): drag the First marker to 07:45 a.m. and read both boxes. Answer: the boxes read 07:45 a.m. and 07:45 hours, because a morning time keeps its digits in the 24-hour format.
Card 2 (practice values): drag the First marker to 04:10 p.m. and turn on Show the 12 added. What does the 24-hour box read? Answer: 16:10 hours, because 4 + 12 = 16 and the minutes stay 10.

Card 3 (practice values): the 24-hour box shows 21:20 hours. Drag the marker to where it goes and type the 12-hour time. Then do the same for 18:05 hours. Answer: 09:20 p.m., because 21 − 12 = 9 and the minutes stay 20, and 06:05 p.m., because 18 − 12 = 6 and the minutes stay 05.

Card 4 (practice values): put the First marker at 09:25 hours and the Second marker at 11:50 hours and read the gap bar. Answer: 2 hours 25 minutes, because 09:25 hours to 11:25 hours is 2 hours and 11:25 hours to 11:50 hours is 25 minutes.

Card 5 (practice values): put the First marker at 08:40 hours and the Second marker at 11:10 hours and read the gap bar. Answer: 2 hours 30 minutes, because 08:40 hours to 09:00 hours is 20 minutes, 09:00 hours to 11:00 hours is 2 hours, 11:00 hours to 11:10 hours is 10 minutes, and 20 + 10 = 30 minutes.

Challenge: 'Fill in the blanks by writing the time in the appropriate format.' The table has the 12-hour format on the left and the 24-hour format on the right: 05:30 a.m. = 05:30 hours; ___ = 08:35 hours; 11:55 a.m. = ___ hours; 02:30 p.m. = 14:30 hours; 05:30 p.m. = ___ hours; 09:35 p.m. = ___ hours. Then 'Match the following.' The 12-hour times 06:30 a.m., 08:45 p.m., 11:45 p.m., 04:30 a.m., 07:30 p.m., 01:30 a.m. are matched to the 24-hour times 01:30 hours, 23:45 hours, 06:30 hours, 20:45 hours, 04:30 hours, 19:30 hours. Answers: 08:35 a.m., 11:55 hours, 17:30 hours and 21:35 hours; 06:30 a.m. with 06:30 hours, 08:45 p.m. with 20:45 hours, 11:45 p.m. with 23:45 hours, 04:30 a.m. with 04:30 hours, 07:30 p.m. with 19:30 hours, 01:30 a.m. with 01:30 hours.

Challenge: 'Raghu left his house at 08:00 hours and arrived at his Nana ji's house at 09:05 hours. How long did he take to reach his house?' Put the markers on the two times and type the answer. Answer: 1 hour 5 minutes, because 08:00 hours to 09:00 hours is 1 hour and 09:00 hours to 09:05 hours is 5 minutes.
feedback: A wrong 24-hour time for a p.m. time gets a soft amber note with the reason, never red, and the +12 bracket lights up: for 05:30 p.m., the hour 5 plus 12 is 17, the minutes stay 30, so 17:30 hours.
A morning time shows its twin: the note points to the a.m. side of the strip and shows the same hour box under the marker, so 07:45 a.m. is 07:45 hours.
A 24-hour time above 12 typed as a morning time gets a note: 21 is more than 12, so the marker is in the moon side of the strip, and 21 − 12 = 9 gives 09:20 p.m.
A wrong gap shows the hops on the gap bar, to the next whole hour, then whole hours, then the rest, with the numbers written on the bar.
A gap typed with minutes above 59 gets a note: minutes on a clock never go past 59, so recount with the hops on the bar.
tool_config.done_when: All 7 cards are done, the table, the six matches and the question about Raghu's trip are correct, and the last card is finished without a bottom-out hint.

hint_ladder.text: What does the card ask: a time in the other format, or the time between two times?

For a p.m. time add 12 to the hour, and for a 24-hour time above 12 take 12 away. A morning time keeps its digits and the minutes never change. For a gap, hop to the next whole hour, then whole hours, then the rest.
Look at the hour of your time. Is it a morning time or a p.m. time? Then add 12 or take 12 away. For a gap, say how many minutes reach the next whole hour.

Worked steps on practice times: 03:20 p.m. is a p.m. time, so 3 + 12 = 15 and it is 15:20 hours. Do the same with your card.

media.context: Racing Seconds. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Show the 12-hour format (a.m., p.m.) and the 24-hour format, both ways: a morning time keeps its digits, a p.m. time adds 12 to the hour, the minutes never change. It works this example: (a) Write 07:45 p.m. in the 24-hour format. (b) Write 16:20 hours in the 12-hour format.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a day has 24 hours, but a 12-hour clock only counts up to 12. How does it tell 05:30 in the morning from 05:30 in the evening? It adds a.m. or p.m. A day has 24 hours, so the 12-hour clock goes round twice. The first round is the morning (a.m.). The second round is the afternoon and evening (p.m.). The 24-hour format counts once, from 00:00 to 24:00. It does not use a.m. or p.m. It writes the word hours after the time. A morning time keeps its digits: 05:30 a.m. is 05:30 hours. For a p.m. time, add 12 to the hour: 02:30 p.m. is 2 + 12 = 14, so it is 14:30 hours. The minutes never change. To go back from a 24-hour time above 12, take 12 away from the hour. Rule: a morning time keeps its digits. For a p.m. time, add 12 to the hour. The minutes stay the same. 1. (a) 07:45 p.m. is a p.m. time, so add 12 to the hour. 2. 7 + 12 = 19. 3. The minutes stay 45, so 07:45 p.m. is 19:45 hours. 4. (b) 16 is more than 12, so it is a p.m. time. Take 12 away from the hour. 5. 16 − 12 = 4. 6. The minutes stay 20, so 16:20 hours is 04:20 p.m. 7. Check: going back, 4 + 12 = 16 and 19 − 12 = 7, so both answers match. Answer: (a) 19:45 hours (b) 04:20 p.m.

steps: The rule: a morning time keeps its digits, and a p.m. time adds 12 to the hour. The minutes never change.
Second row: 08 is less than 12, so 08:35 hours is a morning time, 08:35 a.m.
Third row: 11:55 a.m. is a morning time, so it keeps its digits: 11:55 hours.
Fifth row: 05:30 p.m. is a p.m. time, so add 12 to the hour. 5 + 12 = 17, so it is 17:30 hours.
Sixth row: 09:35 p.m. is a p.m. time, so add 12 to the hour. 9 + 12 = 21, so it is 21:35 hours.
Check: going back, 17 − 12 = 5 and 21 − 12 = 9, so 17:30 hours is 05:30 p.m. and 21:35 hours is 09:35 p.m.
content.answer: Second row: 08:35 a.m. Third row: 11:55 hours. Fifth row: 17:30 hours. Sixth row: 21:35 hours.

content.question: Raghu left his house at 08:00 hours and arrived at his Nana ji's house at 09:05 hours. How long did he take to reach his house?
steps: Raghu left at 08:00 hours and arrived at 09:05 hours.
08:00 hours to 09:00 hours is 1 hour.
09:00 hours to 09:05 hours is 5 minutes.
So Raghu took 1 hour 5 minutes to reach his Nana ji's house.
Check: 08:00 hours plus 1 hour is 09:00 hours, and 09:00 hours plus 5 minutes is 09:05 hours.

content.text:
1. Predict first: two runners both finish a race in 1 minute and a few seconds. Can a clock that shows only minutes tell which of them won?
2. No. Minutes are too big to show a small difference. So we use a smaller unit, the second.
3. 1 minute = 60 seconds. A race time such as 01:48 is read as minutes first, then seconds: 1 minute 48 seconds.
4. If two runners both took 1 minute, compare the extra seconds. The runner with the least time wins, so the smaller number of seconds wins.
5. On the winners' stand, the child with the least time stands first, the child with the next least time stands second, and the child with the next least time stands third.
6. Rule: 1 minute = 60 seconds. In a race the least time wins.

content.text:
Worked example: In a race, Remo's time is 01:48 and Zainab's time is 01:52, in minutes and seconds. Read each time. Who won, and by how many seconds? Change Remo's time to seconds.
1. 01:48 means 1 minute 48 seconds. 01:52 means 1 minute 52 seconds.
2. Both took 1 minute, so compare the seconds. 48 is less than 52.
3. The least time wins, so Remo won.
4. 52 − 48 = 4 seconds, so Remo won by 4 seconds.
5. 1 minute = 60 seconds, so 1 minute 48 seconds = 60 + 48 = 108 seconds.
6. Check: Zainab's 1 minute 52 seconds is 60 + 52 = 112 seconds, and 112 − 108 = 4 seconds.
Answer: Remo won by 4 seconds. His time, 1 minute 48 seconds, is 108 seconds

content.text:
1. Predict first: would you measure blinking your eyes in seconds or in minutes? And melting an ice-cube?
2. 1 minute is 60 seconds. Blinking is over in a moment, far less than 1 minute, so use seconds. Melting an ice-cube takes much longer than 1 minute, so use minutes.
3. Ask one question: is it over in less than 1 minute? If yes, use seconds. If it takes longer than 1 minute, use minutes.
4. This is an estimate, so your answer may be a little different from a friend's answer.
5. Rule: less than 1 minute, use seconds. More than 1 minute, use minutes.

content.text:
Worked example: Choose seconds or minutes for each activity: (a) tying a shoelace (b) boiling an egg (c) saying your name.
1. Ask: is it over in less than 1 minute?
2. (a) Tying a shoelace is over in less than 1 minute, so the unit is seconds.
3. (b) Boiling an egg takes much longer than 1 minute, so the unit is minutes.
4. (c) Saying your name is over in less than 1 minute, so the unit is seconds.
5. Check: 1 minute is 60 seconds, and only boiling an egg takes longer than 60 seconds.
Answer: (a) seconds (b) minutes (c) seconds

steps: For each activity, first write your estimate: how many you think you can do in 1 minute.

Do the activity and count. Write the number you counted as the actual number.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the thin red hand starts on 3 and stops on 8. Have more than 20 seconds passed, or fewer?
2. The thin red hand is the seconds hand. It goes once round the clock in 60 seconds. Each number on the dial is 5 seconds, so 3 is 15 seconds and 8 is 40 seconds.
3. From 3 to 8: 40 − 15 = 25 seconds. That is more than 20 seconds.
4. When the seconds hand has gone once round, the minute hand moves on by one mark. 60 movements of the seconds hand make the minute hand move on by one minute.
5. If the hand goes past 12, count to 12 first and then on. From 8 to 2 is 20 seconds to reach 12 and 10 seconds more. Do not take 2 from 8.
6. Rule: each number is 5 seconds. Count from the start to the end, past 12 if you must.

content.text:
Worked example: Remo timed himself tying his shoe. (a) The seconds hand started on 3 and stopped on 8. How many seconds did he take? (b) On another try it started on 8 and stopped on 2. How many seconds?
1. (a) Each number on the dial is 5 seconds. The start, 3, is 3 × 5 = 15 seconds. The stop, 8, is 8 × 5 = 40 seconds.
2. 40 − 15 = 25 seconds.
3. (b) The start, 8, is 8 × 5 = 40 seconds. From 8 to 12 is 60 − 40 = 20 seconds.
4. From 12 to 2 is 2 × 5 = 10 seconds.
5. 20 + 10 = 30 seconds.
6. Check: 40 seconds and 30 more is 70 seconds, and 70 − 60 = 10, which is the number 2.
Answer: (a) 25 seconds (b) 30 seconds

content.text:
1. Predict first: the seconds hand is on 10 and runs for 25 seconds. Will it stop before 12, or will it go past 12?
2. 10 is 50 seconds. 50 + 25 = 75 seconds, which is more than 60, so the hand goes past 12.
3. Change the seconds into steps of 5: 25 ÷ 5 = 5 steps. Count 5 numbers on from 10: 11, 12, 1, 2, 3. The hand stops on 3.
4. The hand went past 12 once, so the minute hand has moved on by one mark.
5. 60 seconds is one full round. The hand is back on the same number, and the minute hand has moved on by one mark. So the same number at the start and the end does not mean that no time has passed.
6. Rule: change the seconds into steps of 5 and count on from the start. Past 12, the minute hand moves on.

tool_config.idea: Run the seconds hand, mark where it started, and read how many seconds have passed from the numbers it moved over, five seconds for each number; then drag the seconds hand to the place where it stops after a given number of seconds, and see the minute hand step on when the hand goes once round.
tool_config.screen: The timing board beside the school track, drawn as a warm, polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation: a post with one very large analogue clock on it, the largest thing on screen, with a dark teal rim, a pale face, every number from 1 to 12, 60 small marks, a short blue hour hand, a long orange minute hand and a thin red seconds hand. A ring of small labels 5, 10, 15, ..., 60 sits just outside the dial, one label beside each number. A pale copy of the seconds hand, named the start ghost, stays where the run began. A pale red stretch is shaded round the dial from the start ghost to the seconds hand. A box named Seconds counted shows the number of seconds, and a small step light beside the minute hand blinks when the seconds hand passes 12 and the minute hand moves on by one mark. Controls: Go (the seconds hand runs, one mark at a time, at a slow speed so it can be watched) and Stop, Mark start, a button Run for N seconds on the cards that say how many seconds, drag the seconds hand with a finger, type a number of seconds with a large number pad, and Check. On the book's cards two clocks sit side by side, a left clock and a right clock, as in the pictures, and the student types the seconds taken or drags the missing seconds hand onto the right clock. Fixed controls: Hint, Retry (returns the hand to the start of this card), Reset (returns the clock to 12), Back and Next in the same places on every card, and 7 progress dots, with a one-sentence instruction strip at the top and a counter showing the card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at the seconds hand on 3 and then on 8, as in the video. Press Go and watch the red hand. Say how many seconds have passed when it stops.

Run the seconds hand and read the seconds taken from the start ghost, run it past 12 and watch the minute hand step on, and drag the seconds hand to where it stops after a number of seconds (practice values).
Read the four pairs of clocks of the book and write the seconds taken, then draw the missing seconds hand on the right clock of the four pairs of the second book box.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): the seconds hand starts on 12. Press Go and press Stop when the hand is on 3. How many seconds have passed? Answer: 15 seconds, because each number is 5 seconds and 3 × 5 = 15.

Card 2 (practice values): the seconds hand starts on 2. Mark the start, press Go and press Stop on 11. How many seconds? Answer: 45 seconds, because 2 is 10 seconds, 11 is 55 seconds and 55 − 10 = 45.

Card 3 (practice values): the seconds hand starts on 10 and stops on 4, after it has gone past 12. Watch the step light. How many seconds? Answer: 30 seconds, because from 10 to 12 is 60 − 50 = 10 seconds, from 12 to 4 is 4 × 5 = 20 seconds, and 10 + 20 = 30 seconds. The minute hand moved on by one mark.

Card 4 (practice values): the seconds hand is on 7. It runs for 40 seconds. Drag the seconds hand to where it stops and say what the minute hand does. Answer: on 3, because 7 is 35 seconds, 35 + 40 = 75, 75 − 60 = 15 seconds, and 15 ÷ 5 = 3; the hand went past 12 once, so the minute hand moves on by one mark.

Card 5 (practice values): the seconds hand starts on 5. Press Run for 60 seconds. Where does the hand stop and what happens to the minute hand? Answer: the hand is back on 5 and the minute hand has moved on by one mark, because one full round is 60 seconds, which is 1 minute.

Challenge: 'Observe the clocks and fill in the blanks.' Four pairs of clocks, each with the seconds hand on the left clock and on the right clock: 'Rani took ___ seconds to get out of her bed.' (the seconds hand on 12 and then on 6), 'Raghav took ___ seconds to move from his room to the kitchen.' (on 12 and then on 7), 'Ritu took ___ seconds to pick up a piece of paper from the floor.' (on 9 and then on 12), 'Raghu took ___ seconds to wash his spoon and plate.' (on 5 both times, with the minute hand one mark on). Answers: 30 seconds, 35 seconds, 15 seconds and 60 seconds.

Challenge: 'Draw the missing seconds hand on the clocks on the right side.' Four pairs of clocks, the right clock of each with no seconds hand: 'Raghu took 20 seconds to read a sentence in his book.' (the left hand on 12), 'Rani took 30 seconds to color a rectangle.' (on 12), 'Raghav took 60 seconds to move from his home to the garden.' (on 9), 'Ritu took 40 seconds to wash a plate.' (on 11). Answers: the hand on 4, on 6, on 9 again with the minute hand one mark on, and on 7 with the minute hand one mark on.
feedback: The seconds taken are shown on the stretch as the hand moves, so the student sees the count grow in fives: 5, 10, 15, and the Seconds counted box gives the same number.
A wrong number of seconds gets a soft amber note with the reason, never red: from 9 to 12 the hand passes 3 numbers, so 3 × 5 = 15 seconds, and the stretch is shaded on the clock.

A hand dragged to the wrong number is not moved back by the tool: the stretch from the start to the dragged hand is shaded and its seconds are written, and the student sees that they do not match the seconds asked for.
When the hand goes past 12 the step light blinks and a note says that the minute hand moves on by one mark each time the seconds hand goes once round, and that 60 seconds is 1 minute.
A hand on the same number at the start and the end gets a note to look at the minute hand: if it has moved on by one mark, one full round has passed, which is 60 seconds.

content.text:
1. Predict first: 5 hours 25 minutes in minutes. Is it more than 300 minutes, or less?
2. 1 hour = 60 minutes. On a double number line the hours are above and the minutes are below, and every hour is 60 minutes further along.
3. Zainab: 1 hour is 60 minutes, so 2 hours is 2 × 60 = 120 minutes. Remo goes the other way: 180 minutes = 3 hours, because 3 × 60 = 180.
4. Hours and minutes to minutes: change the hours to minutes, then add the minutes. 5 hours 25 minutes is 5 × 60 + 25 = 325 minutes. That is more than 300.
5. Minutes to hours and minutes: find how many whole groups of 60 fit, and keep what is left. In 370 minutes, 60 × 6 = 360, so there are 6 hours and 370 − 360 = 10 minutes left.
6. Rule: hours to minutes, multiply by 60. Minutes to hours, find the whole groups of 60 and keep the rest.

content.text:
Worked example: (a) Change 5 hours 25 minutes to minutes. (b) Change 370 minutes to hours and minutes.
1. (a) 1 hour = 60 minutes, so 5 hours = 5 × 60 = 300 minutes.
2. 300 + 25 = 325 minutes.
3. (b) 60 × 6 = 360 and 60 × 7 = 420. 370 is between them, so there are 6 whole hours.
4. 370 − 360 = 10 minutes are left.
5. So 370 minutes = 6 hours 10 minutes.
6. Check: 6 × 60 = 360 and 360 + 10 = 370.
Answer: (a) 325 minutes (b) 6 hours 10 minutes

content.text:
1. Predict first: 4 minutes 30 seconds in seconds. Is it more than 240 seconds, or less?
2. 1 minute = 60 seconds. The second double number line has the minutes above and the seconds below. 1 minute is 60 seconds, so 5 minutes is 5 × 60 = 300 seconds.
3. Minutes and seconds to seconds: change the minutes to seconds, then add the seconds. 4 minutes 30 seconds is 4 × 60 + 30 = 270 seconds. That is more than 240.
4. Seconds to minutes and seconds: find how many whole groups of 60 fit, and keep what is left. In 400 seconds, 60 × 6 = 360, so there are 6 minutes and 400 − 360 = 40 seconds left.
5. Rule: minutes to seconds, multiply by 60. Seconds to minutes, find the whole groups of 60 and keep the rest.

media.title: Time Converter Line

tool_config.title: Time Converter Line
tool_config.idea: Change one unit of time into the next on a double number line: hours into minutes, and minutes into seconds, where every step multiplies by 60, and back again by finding how many whole groups of 60 fit and what is left.
tool_config.screen: The school notice board, drawn as a warm, polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation: a long strip of paper pinned across the board carries a double number line, the largest thing on screen. The top line and the bottom line run side by side with aligned ticks, one tick below each tick. A mode switch above the strip reads Hours and minutes or Minutes and seconds: in the first mode the top line shows hours (0 to 12) and the bottom line minutes (0 to 720), in the second the top line shows minutes (0 to 25) and the bottom line seconds (0 to 1500). A bright slider with a handle sits on both lines at once and moves along them, snapping to a whole number on the top line, with the two numbers it points at shown in two read-out boxes. Curved arrows named × 60, × 2 and × 5 can be shown above the line with a button Show × 60. Blank ticks show a number box: tapping a box opens a large number pad. A groups of 60 strip under the bottom line can be switched on: it cuts the bottom number into whole blocks of 60 and shows the part that is left over as a short block. Controls: drag the slider, tap the mode switch, tap a blank box and type, tap Show × 60 and the groups of 60 switch, and tap Check. For a conversion card with hours and minutes, a sentence with blanks sits under the line, for example 1 hour 10 minutes = ___ minutes, and the student types the blanks. Fixed controls: Hint, Retry (clears the boxes of this card), Reset (restores the line), Back and Next in the same places on every card, and 7 progress dots, with a one-sentence instruction strip at the top and a counter showing the card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at the double number line with 1 hour above 60 minutes and 2 hours above 120 minutes, as in the video. Slide to 3 hours and read the minutes.

Slide along the line and read the minutes for a number of hours, type the minutes for hours and minutes together, find the hours and minutes for a number of minutes with the groups of 60 strip, and then do the same with minutes and seconds (practice values).
Fill the blanks of the book's two double number lines and its conversions, and find the total time Raghav studied.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): slide to 5 hours and read the minutes, then slide to 10 hours. Answer: 300 minutes and 600 minutes, because 5 × 60 = 300 and 10 × 60 = 600.
Card 2 (practice values): type the minutes for 6 hours 40 minutes. Answer: 400 minutes, because 6 × 60 = 360 and 360 + 40 = 400.
Card 3 (practice values): the line shows 470 minutes. Switch on the groups of 60 strip and type the hours and the minutes. Answer: 7 hours 50 minutes, because 60 × 7 = 420 and 470 − 420 = 50.

Card 4 (practice values): switch to Minutes and seconds, slide to 3 minutes and read the seconds, then type the seconds for 7 minutes 20 seconds. Answer: 180 seconds, and 440 seconds, because 3 × 60 = 180, 7 × 60 = 420 and 420 + 20 = 440.
Card 5 (practice values): the line shows 500 seconds. Switch on the groups of 60 strip and type the minutes and the seconds. Answer: 8 minutes 20 seconds, because 60 × 8 = 480 and 500 − 480 = 20.

A minutes part above 59 in an answer such as 1 hour 75 minutes gets a note: 75 minutes is 1 hour 15 minutes, so cut the hours out first.

media.title: Hours and Minutes
media.context: Racing Seconds. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Show how to change hours and minutes to minutes and back, with a double number line: multiply by 60, or find the whole groups of 60. It works this example: (a) Change 5 hours 25 minutes to minutes. (b) Change 370 minutes to hours and minutes.
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: 5 hours 25 minutes in minutes. Is it more than 300 minutes, or less? 1 hour = 60 minutes. On a double number line the hours are above and the minutes are below, and every hour is 60 minutes further along. Zainab: 1 hour is 60 minutes, so 2 hours is 2 × 60 = 120 minutes. Remo goes the other way: 180 minutes = 3 hours, because 3 × 60 = 180. Hours and minutes to minutes: change the hours to minutes, then add the minutes. 5 hours 25 minutes is 5 × 60 + 25 = 325 minutes. That is more than 300. Minutes to hours and minutes: find how many whole groups of 60 fit, and keep what is left. In 370 minutes, 60 × 6 = 360, so there are 6 hours and 370 − 360 = 10 minutes left. Rule: hours to minutes, multiply by 60. Minutes to hours, find the whole groups of 60 and keep the rest. 1. (a) 1 hour = 60 minutes, so 5 hours = 5 × 60 = 300 minutes. 2. 300 + 25 = 325 minutes. 3. (b) 60 × 6 = 360 and 60 × 7 = 420. 370 is between them, so there are 6 whole hours. 4. 370 − 360 = 10 minutes are left. 5. So 370 minutes = 6 hours 10 minutes. 6. Check: 6 × 60 = 360 and 360 + 10 = 370. Answer: (a) 325 minutes (b) 6 hours 10 minutes

content.question: Raghav studies Mathematics, English, Hindi, and The World Around Us subjects. He took 50 minutes to study each of the subjects. Find the total time taken in hours and minutes. Share your strategies with your class.
steps: There are 4 subjects and each took 50 minutes.
4 × 50 = 200 minutes.
60 × 3 = 180 minutes, which is 3 hours, and 200 − 180 = 20 minutes are left.
So the total time is 3 hours 20 minutes.
Another strategy: 50 + 50 = 100 minutes is 1 hour 40 minutes for 2 subjects, and 1 hour 40 minutes twice is 2 hours 80 minutes, which is 3 hours 20 minutes.
Check: 3 × 60 + 20 = 200 minutes.
content.answer: 3 hours 20 minutes. Your strategy may differ

content.text:
1. Predict first: Zainab starts painting at 03:20 p.m. and paints for 1 hour 50 minutes. Will she stop before 05:00 p.m., or after it?
2. Add the hours first. 03:20 p.m. plus 1 hour is 04:20 p.m.
3. Then add the minutes in easy hops. From 04:20 p.m. it is 60 − 20 = 40 minutes to 05:00 p.m. 50 − 40 = 10 minutes are left, so go 10 minutes past 05:00 p.m. That is 05:10 p.m., after 05:00 p.m.
4. Minutes on a clock never go past 59. After 60 minutes the hour goes up by 1, so 04:20 p.m. plus 50 minutes is not 04:70 p.m.
5. Do these in your head with hops, not by writing the numbers in columns.
6. Rule: add the hours, then hop to the next whole hour, then add the minutes left.

Worked example: Zainab starts painting at 03:20 p.m. and paints for 1 hour 50 minutes. At what time does she stop?
1. Add the hours first: 03:20 p.m. plus 1 hour is 04:20 p.m.

3. 50 − 40 = 10 minutes are left to add.

5. So Zainab stops at 05:10 p.m.
6. Check by going back: 05:10 p.m. minus 1 hour is 04:10 p.m., and 04:10 p.m. minus 50 minutes is 03:20 p.m.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Remo finished reading at 08:15 p.m. after reading for 2 hours 40 minutes. Did he start before 06:00 p.m., or after it?
2. Go back the hours first. 08:15 p.m. minus 2 hours is 06:15 p.m.
3. Then go back the minutes in easy hops. From 06:15 p.m. back to 06:00 p.m. is 15 minutes. 40 − 15 = 25 minutes are left, so go 25 minutes before 06:00 p.m. That is 05:35 p.m., before 06:00 p.m.
4. Going back is the same hops the other way round.
5. Check by going forward: 05:35 p.m. plus 2 hours 40 minutes should give 08:15 p.m.
6. Rule: go back the hours, then hop back to the whole hour, then go back the minutes left.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a bus leaves at 10:40 a.m. and the trip takes 3 hours 30 minutes. Will it arrive in the morning (a.m.) or in the afternoon (p.m.)?
2. When the clock goes past 12 noon, the a.m. changes to p.m. This bus passes 12 noon, so it arrives in the afternoon.
3. Midnight is the end of the day, 24:00 hours. A new day begins at 00:00 hours.
4. To cross noon or midnight, change to the 24-hour clock and add there. 10:40 a.m. is 10:40 hours. 10:40 hours plus 3 hours 30 minutes is 14:10 hours, and 14 − 12 = 2, so it is 02:10 p.m.
5. If the 24-hour time goes above 24:00 hours, take 24 away. 28:00 hours is 28 − 24 = 4, so it is 04:00 hours the next day.
6. Rule: use the 24-hour clock to cross noon and midnight. A time above 24:00 hours is in the next day.

content.text:
Worked example: (a) A bus leaves at 10:40 a.m. and the trip takes 3 hours 30 minutes. When does it arrive? (b) A train leaves at 10:15 p.m. and the journey takes 5 hours 45 minutes. When does it arrive?
1. (a) 10:40 a.m. is a morning time, so it is 10:40 hours.
2. 10:40 hours plus 3 hours is 13:40 hours.
3. From 13:40 hours to 14:00 hours is 20 minutes, and 30 − 20 = 10 minutes are left, so 14:10 hours.
4. 14 − 12 = 2, so 14:10 hours is 02:10 p.m. The clock passed 12 noon, so a.m. changed to p.m.
5. (b) 10:15 p.m. is 10 + 12 = 22, so it is 22:15 hours.
6. 22:15 hours plus 5 hours is 27:15 hours. 27:15 hours plus 45 minutes is 28:00 hours, because 15 + 45 = 60 minutes make 1 more hour.
7. A day ends at 24:00 hours, so take 24 away: 28 − 24 = 4. The train arrives at 04:00 hours, which is 04:00 a.m. the next day.
8. Check: 10:15 p.m. to midnight is 1 hour 45 minutes, and midnight to 04:00 a.m. is 4 hours. 1 hour 45 minutes plus 4 hours is 5 hours 45 minutes.
Answer: (a) 02:10 p.m. (b) 04:00 a.m. the next day

media.title: Time Jumper

tool_config.title: Time Jumper
tool_config.idea: Find the time after, or before, a time by hopping along a time line, the hours first and then the minutes up to the next whole hour, and see the a.m. and p.m. change at 12 noon and a new day begin after midnight.
tool_config.screen: The school playground, drawn as a warm, polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation: a long hopscotch line chalked on the ground is a time line and is the largest thing on screen. The line has a tall tick for every whole hour and 5 small ticks of 5 minutes between them, with the hours labelled; the left part of the line has a sun and the label a.m., the right part has a moon and the label p.m., 12 noon has a bright marker, and after 12 midnight a band named Next day starts. A small flag stands at the start time and a child's shoe hops from the flag to the landing time. Jump cards sit in a tray under the line: 1 hour, 30 minutes, 10 minutes, 5 minutes and 1 minute, each with a Forward and a Back side. A read-out beside the line shows the landing time in the 12-hour format (hh:mm a.m. or p.m.) and a second read-out shows the 24-hour time (hh:mm hours); a small clock with a blue hour hand and an orange minute hand follows the landing time. Controls: drag a jump card onto the line (the shoe hops by that much and the landing time updates), tap Undo to take the last jump off, tap Forward or Back to choose the direction of the card, type the end time with a large number pad, and tap Check. Fixed controls: Hint, Retry (returns the shoe to the start of this card), Reset (clears every jump), Back and Next in the same places on every card, and 7 progress dots, with a one-sentence instruction strip at the top and a counter showing the card number out of 7.
student_does: Look at the flag at 03:20 p.m. and one jump of 1 hour, as in the video. Say where the shoe lands and what is left to add.
Drag jump cards to find the time after a time, then the time before a time, then a time after that passes 12 noon, and one that passes midnight (practice values).
Solve the book's time problems by hopping and type each time.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): the flag is at 02:10 p.m. Hop forward 1 hour 35 minutes with an hour card and minute cards. Where does the shoe land? Answer: 03:45 p.m., because 02:10 p.m. plus 1 hour is 03:10 p.m. and 03:10 p.m. plus 35 minutes is 03:45 p.m.

Card 2 (practice values): the flag is at 07:50 p.m. Hop back 2 hours 20 minutes. Where does the shoe land? Answer: 05:30 p.m., because 07:50 p.m. minus 2 hours is 05:50 p.m. and 05:50 p.m. minus 20 minutes is 05:30 p.m.

Card 3 (practice values): the flag is at 11:25 a.m. Hop forward 1 hour 50 minutes and watch 12 noon. Where does the shoe land? Answer: 01:15 p.m., because 11:25 a.m. plus 1 hour is 12:25 p.m. and 12:25 p.m. plus 50 minutes is 01:15 p.m. The a.m. changed to p.m. at 12 noon.

Card 4 (practice values): the flag is at 11:10 p.m. Hop forward 3 hours 20 minutes and watch midnight. Where does the shoe land? Answer: 02:30 a.m. the next day, because 23:10 hours plus 3 hours 20 minutes is 26:30 hours, and 26 − 24 = 2.

Card 5 (practice values): the flag is at 04:40 p.m. and the shoe has to land on 06:15 p.m. Choose the jump cards. Answer: 1 hour 35 minutes, for example 20 minutes to 05:00 p.m., 1 hour to 06:00 p.m. and 15 minutes to 06:15 p.m., and 20 + 15 = 35 minutes.

Challenge: 'Jyoti went to play at 06:15 PM. She came back after 1 hour 45 minutes. At what time did she reach home?' 'Ragini took 1 hour 10 minutes to do her homework. She finished it at 09:40 PM. What time did she start?' 'A group of children left for a picnic at 08:30 AM. They returned after 4 hours and 10 minutes. At what time did they return?' 'Raji started her homework at 06:00 PM. She finished her homework in 1 hour 30 minutes. At what time did she finish?' 'Alya goes out to play at 05:30 PM and comes back after 1 hour 10 minutes. At what time does she come back?' Answers: 08:00 PM, 08:30 PM, 12:40 PM, 07:30 PM and 06:40 PM.

Challenge: 'If the lunch break of a school starts at 12:30 PM and ends in 35 minutes, what time will lunch end?' 'It is 08:35 PM right now. What time will it be after 8 hours and 25 minutes?' Answers: 01:05 PM, and 05:00 AM the next day, because 20:35 hours plus 8 hours 25 minutes is 29:00 hours and 29 − 24 = 5.
feedback: A jump makes the shoe hop and the landing time update at once, with the 24-hour time beside it, so the student sees what each hop does.
A wrong end time gets a soft amber note with the reason, never red: from 07:15 PM, 45 minutes reach 08:00 PM, not 07:60 PM, because minutes on a clock never go past 59.
When the shoe passes 12 noon the a.m. sun changes to the p.m. moon with a short note, and when it passes midnight the Next day band lights up and the 24-hour read-out goes back to 00:00 hours.
A time typed with the wrong a.m. or p.m. gets a note that points to the sun and moon on the line: after 12 noon the time is p.m.
A backward hop typed as a forward hop gets a note: the time before is earlier on the line, so the shoe hops to the left.

Card 4 (practice values): the flag is at 11:10 p.m. Hop forward 3 hours 20 minutes and watch midnight. Where does the shoe land? Answer: 02:30 a.m. the next day, because 23:10 hours plus 3 hours 20 minutes is 26:30 hours, and 26 − 24 = 2.

Card 5 (practice values): the flag is at 04:40 p.m. and the shoe has to land on 06:15 p.m. Choose the jump cards. Answer: 1 hour 35 minutes, for example 20 minutes to 05:00 p.m., 1 hour to 06:00 p.m. and 15 minutes to 06:15 p.m., and 20 + 15 = 35 minutes.

Challenge: 'Jyoti went to play at 06:15 PM. She came back after 1 hour 45 minutes. At what time did she reach home?' 'Ragini took 1 hour 10 minutes to do her homework. She finished it at 09:40 PM. What time did she start?' 'A group of children left for a picnic at 08:30 AM. They returned after 4 hours and 10 minutes. At what time did they return?' 'Raji started her homework at 06:00 PM. She finished her homework in 1 hour 30 minutes. At what time did she finish?' 'Alya goes out to play at 05:30 PM and comes back after 1 hour 10 minutes. At what time does she come back?' Answers: 08:00 PM, 08:30 PM, 12:40 PM, 07:30 PM and 06:40 PM.

Challenge: 'If the lunch break of a school starts at 12:30 PM and ends in 35 minutes, what time will lunch end?' 'It is 08:35 PM right now. What time will it be after 8 hours and 25 minutes?' Answers: 01:05 PM, and 05:00 AM the next day, because 20:35 hours plus 8 hours 25 minutes is 29:00 hours and 29 − 24 = 5.

media.description: Concept video: Show how to find the time after a start time: add the hours, then hop to the next whole hour and add the minutes left. It works this example: Zainab starts painting at 03:20 p.m. and paints for 1 hour 50 minutes. At what time does she stop?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: Zainab starts painting at 03:20 p.m. and paints for 1 hour 50 minutes. Will she stop before 05:00 p.m., or after it? Add the hours first. 03:20 p.m. plus 1 hour is 04:20 p.m. Then add the minutes in easy hops. From 04:20 p.m. it is 60 − 20 = 40 minutes to 05:00 p.m. 50 − 40 = 10 minutes are left, so go 10 minutes past 05:00 p.m. That is 05:10 p.m., after 05:00 p.m. Minutes on a clock never go past 59. After 60 minutes the hour goes up by 1, so 04:20 p.m. plus 50 minutes is not 04:70 p.m. Do these in your head with hops, not by writing the numbers in columns. Rule: add the hours, then hop to the next whole hour, then add the minutes left. 1. Add the hours first: 03:20 p.m. plus 1 hour is 04:20 p.m. 2. From 04:20 p.m. to 05:00 p.m. is 60 − 20 = 40 minutes. 3. 50 − 40 = 10 minutes are left to add. 4. 05:00 p.m. plus 10 minutes is 05:10 p.m. 5. So Zainab stops at 05:10 p.m. 6. Check by going back: 05:10 p.m. minus 1 hour is 04:10 p.m., and 04:10 p.m. minus 50 minutes is 03:20 p.m. Answer: 05:10 p.m.

media.title: Crossing Noon and Midnight
media.context: Racing Seconds. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Show how to find a time when the time passes 12 noon or midnight, using the 24-hour clock and taking 24 away from a time above 24:00 hours. It works this example: (a) A bus leaves at 10:40 a.m. and the trip takes 3 hours 30 minutes. When does it arrive? (b) A train leaves at 10:15 p.m. and the journey takes 5 hours 45 minutes. When does it arrive?
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a bus leaves at 10:40 a.m. and the trip takes 3 hours 30 minutes. Will it arrive in the morning (a.m.) or in the afternoon (p.m.)? When the clock goes past 12 noon, the a.m. changes to p.m. This bus passes 12 noon, so it arrives in the afternoon. Midnight is the end of the day, 24:00 hours. A new day begins at 00:00 hours. To cross noon or midnight, change to the 24-hour clock and add there. 10:40 a.m. is 10:40 hours. 10:40 hours plus 3 hours 30 minutes is 14:10 hours, and 14 − 12 = 2, so it is 02:10 p.m. If the 24-hour time goes above 24:00 hours, take 24 away. 28:00 hours is 28 − 24 = 4, so it is 04:00 hours the next day. Rule: use the 24-hour clock to cross noon and midnight. A time above 24:00 hours is in the next day. 1. (a) 10:40 a.m. is a morning time, so it is 10:40 hours. 2. 10:40 hours plus 3 hours is 13:40 hours. 3. From 13:40 hours to 14:00 hours is 20 minutes, and 30 − 20 = 10 minutes are left, so 14:10 hours. 4. 14 − 12 = 2, so 14:10 hours is 02:10 p.m. The clock passed 12 noon, so a.m. changed to p.m. 5. (b) 10:15 p.m. is 10 + 12 = 22, so it is 22:15 hours. 6. 22:15 hours plus 5 hours is 27:15 hours. 27:15 hours plus 45 minutes is 28:00 hours, because 15 + 45 = 60 minutes make 1 more hour. 7. A day ends at 24:00 hours, so take 24 away: 28 − 24 = 4. The train arrives at 04:00 hours, which is 04:00 a.m. the next day. 8. Check: 10:15 p.m. to midnight is 1 hour 45 minutes, and midnight to 04:00 a.m. is 4 hours. 1 hour 45 minutes plus 4 hours is 5 hours 45 minutes. Answer: (a) 02:10 p.m. (b) 04:00 a.m. the next day

steps: 08:35 PM is a p.m. time, so add 12 to the hour: 8 + 12 = 20, and it is 20:35 hours.
Add the 25 minutes first: 20:35 hours plus 25 minutes is 21:00 hours.
Add the 8 hours: 21:00 hours plus 8 hours is 29:00 hours.
A day ends at 24:00 hours, so take 24 away: 29 − 24 = 5. The time is 05:00 hours the next day.
05:00 hours is a morning time, so it is 05:00 AM the next day.
Check: 08:35 PM to midnight is 3 hours 25 minutes, and midnight to 05:00 AM is 5 hours. 3 hours 25 minutes plus 5 hours is 8 hours 25 minutes.

Check: 08:35 PM to midnight is 3 hours 25 minutes, and midnight to 05:00 AM is 5 hours. 3 hours 25 minutes plus 5 hours is 8 hours 25 minutes. Answer: 05:00 AM the next day

content.text:
1. Predict first: you have walked through a whole school day of time. Can you say one idea from each stop, from Raghav's yoga clocks to the time jumps? Read the lines below and tick each idea you remembered.
2. Time elapsed: start at the earlier time and count up to the later time in easy hops. 04:25 p.m. to 05:10 p.m. is 35 minutes to reach 05:00 p.m. and 10 minutes more, which is 45 minutes.
3. Check: how long is it from 07:20 a.m. to 10:50 a.m.? It is 3 hours 30 minutes, because 07:20 a.m. to 10:20 a.m. is 3 hours and 10:20 a.m. to 10:50 a.m. is 30 minutes.
4. Comparing times taken: compare the hours first, then the minutes. 2 hours 5 minutes is more than 1 hour 50 minutes, because 2 hours is more than 1 hour.
5. Two formats: a morning time keeps its digits and a p.m. time adds 12 to the hour. 07:45 p.m. is 19:45 hours, because 7 + 12 = 19.
6. Check: what is 16:20 hours in the 12-hour format? It is 04:20 p.m., because 16 − 12 = 4.
7. Time between in 24-hour time: go to the next whole hour, add the whole hours, then the rest. 13:40 hours to 16:15 hours is 20 minutes, 2 hours and 15 minutes, which is 2 hours 35 minutes.
8. Seconds: 1 minute = 60 seconds. 01:48 is 1 minute 48 seconds, which is 60 + 48 = 108 seconds. In a race the least time wins.
9. Seconds or minutes: if an activity is over in less than 1 minute, use seconds, otherwise use minutes. Tying a shoelace is seconds. Boiling an egg is minutes.
10. The seconds hand: each number on the dial is 5 seconds, and one full round is 60 seconds, which moves the minute hand on by one mark. From 3 to 8 is 40 − 15 = 25 seconds.
11. Check: the seconds hand is on 10 and runs for 25 seconds. Where does it stop? On 3, because 50 + 25 = 75, and 75 − 60 = 15 seconds is the number 3.
12. Changing units: hours to minutes, multiply by 60. 5 hours 25 minutes is 5 × 60 + 25 = 325 minutes. Minutes to seconds is the same: 4 minutes 30 seconds is 4 × 60 + 30 = 270 seconds.
13. Check: how many hours and minutes are 370 minutes? It is 6 hours 10 minutes, because 60 × 6 = 360 and 370 − 360 = 10.
14. Time after and time before: add or take away the hours first, then hop to the whole hour and do the minutes left. 03:20 p.m. plus 1 hour 50 minutes is 05:10 p.m., and 08:15 p.m. minus 2 hours 40 minutes is 05:35 p.m.
15. Noon and midnight: at 12 noon a.m. changes to p.m. A day ends at 24:00 hours, so 28:00 hours is 28 − 24 = 4, which is 04:00 a.m. the next day.
16. Check: what is 10:40 a.m. plus 3 hours 30 minutes? It is 02:10 p.m., because the time is 14:10 hours and 14 − 12 = 2.

objectives.objective_text: Students find the time elapsed between two clock times by counting up in easy hops, and say it in hours and minutes.

objectives.objective_text: Students compare times taken that are given in hours and minutes, and say which is the longest and which is the least.
objectives.strand_name: Clock Time, Time Elapsed and Two Ways to Write the Time

objectives.objective_text: Students read two clocks to find the start time, the finish time and how long Raghav took, find how long it is between two times, and compare times taken in hours and minutes.
objectives.strand_name: Clock Time, Time Elapsed and Two Ways to Write the Time

objectives.objective_text: Students write a time in the 12-hour format and in the 24-hour format, changing it both ways.
objectives.strand_name: Clock Time, Time Elapsed and Two Ways to Write the Time

objectives.objective_text: Students find how long it is between two 24-hour times by hopping to the next whole hour, then whole hours, then the rest, and say it in hours and minutes.
objectives.strand_name: Clock Time, Time Elapsed and Two Ways to Write the Time

objectives.objective_text: Students write times in the 12-hour and 24-hour formats, match them, and find the time between two 24-hour times.
objectives.strand_name: Clock Time, Time Elapsed and Two Ways to Write the Time

objectives.objective_text: Students read a race time such as 01:48 as minutes and seconds, change 1 minute and some seconds to seconds, and say which of two race times is the least.
Students choose seconds or minutes as the unit for an activity by asking whether it is over in less than 1 minute, and say why.
Students read the times on the winners' stand in minutes and seconds, name the child who won the race, and estimate whether an activity takes seconds or minutes.
Students read the seconds hand on two clocks to find the seconds taken, counting past 12 when the hand goes round, and say what happens to the minute hand.
Students draw the seconds hand where it stops after a given number of seconds by changing the seconds into steps of 5, and say when the minute hand moves on.
Students read the seconds hand on pairs of clocks to find the seconds taken, and draw the missing seconds hand after a given number of seconds.
Students change hours and minutes to minutes by multiplying the hours by 60, and change minutes to hours and minutes by finding the whole groups of 60.
objectives.strand_name: Changing Units and Solving Time Problems

objectives.objective_text: Students change minutes and seconds to seconds by multiplying the minutes by 60, and change seconds to minutes and seconds by finding the whole groups of 60.
objectives.strand_name: Changing Units and Solving Time Problems

objectives.objective_text: Students fill the blanks of a double number line, and change hours to minutes, minutes to hours and minutes, minutes to seconds and seconds to minutes and seconds.
objectives.strand_name: Changing Units and Solving Time Problems

objectives.objective_text: Students find the time after a start time by adding the hours first and then the minutes in easy hops, without writing minutes above 59.
objectives.strand_name: Changing Units and Solving Time Problems

objectives.objective_text: Students find the start time before a finish time by going back the hours first and then the minutes in easy hops, and check by going forward.
objectives.strand_name: Changing Units and Solving Time Problems

objectives.objective_text: Students find the time after a start time when the time crosses 12 noon or midnight, using the 24-hour clock, and say the new time with a.m. or p.m.
objectives.strand_name: Changing Units and Solving Time Problems

objectives.objective_text: Students find the time after and the time before a given time with hops of hours and minutes, including across 12 noon and midnight, in the book's time problems.
